Is your S-corp salary defensible — and what does closing the gap cost?

A single-shareholder S-corp that also performs services for the business must pay a "reasonable" W-2 salary before taking any profit out as a distribution. There is no IRS safe-harbor percentage — the test is a comparable-wage comparison: what an unrelated employer would pay someone else to do your job, for your hours. Enter your own numbers below and see where you stand, and what raising salary would cost in FICA tax.

After using this, you can now see whether your planned S-corp salary is defensible against the actual test the IRS and courts apply, and exactly how much closing the gap costs in FICA tax — which used to mean paying $200-900 for a third-party reasonable-compensation report or guessing at a mythical "60/40 rule" that isn't an IRS rule at all. See why the IRS cares, how this compares to a paid reasonable-compensation report, or how this compares to just picking a round number.

Lowering your salary also raises your Section 199A QBI deduction (wages reduce QBI) — see the QBI deduction calculator for that side of the same pass-through income, and weigh it against the audit-risk flag below before deciding. Own your home? See what renting it to your business for up to 14 days saves with the Augusta rule calculator.

Your numbers

"Compensation pool" is your S-corp's net ordinary income for the year, before your own wages are subtracted. The comparable-wage figure is one you supply — from BLS OEWS wage data, a trade salary survey, or your own judgment of what a competing employer would pay for this exact role and these exact hours.

Result

Enter your numbers above and choose Assess.

—Comparable-wage floor (hours-adjusted)
—Implied distribution at your planned salary
—Combined FICA tax at your planned salary
—Extra FICA to raise salary to the floor

Nine-factor documentation checklist

Courts and the IRS weigh a multi-factor test rather than one number (see the explainer page for the case law). This calculator does not score or sum these into a figure — that would overstate what arithmetic can settle. Print this page or copy your answers into your own file as evidence of how the number above was reached.

Every figure you enter stays on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Usage counts contain only feature names and are never sent anywhere.

Common questions

What is "reasonable compensation" for an S-corp owner?

A shareholder of an S-corp who also performs services for the business must be paid a reasonable salary as W-2 wages before any profit is distributed to them. The IRS and the courts test this by comparing your pay to what an unrelated employer would pay someone else to do the same job, for the same hours — not by any fixed percentage of profit.

Is there an IRS safe-harbor percentage, like paying yourself 60% of profit as salary?

No. The IRS has never published a safe-harbor percentage, and the "60/40" or "1/3" rules of thumb circulating online are informal guidance from advisors, not an IRS rule. This calculator does not use a percentage rule; it compares your planned salary to a comparable-wage figure you supply for your own role and hours, which is the test actually applied in litigated cases.

What happens if I pay myself too little salary and take the rest as distributions?

The IRS can recharacterize part of your distributions as wages, assess back payroll tax (both the employer and employee shares of FICA), plus penalties and interest. Watson v. Commissioner (8th Cir. 2012) is the leading case: a $24,000 salary against roughly $200,000–274,000 of annual profit was recharacterized to $91,044.

Can my S-corp pay me more salary than it actually earned this year?

A corporation is not generally expected to pay out more in salary than it earned in a lean year — the reasonable-compensation rule targets disguised distributions from profit that exists, not a shortfall when there isn't any. If your comparable-wage figure exceeds what the business made, that is a signal to talk to your own preparer about the options, not a hard floor this calculator enforces.

Why does raising my salary cost more in FICA tax?

W-2 salary is subject to combined Social Security and Medicare tax (FICA) — 15.3% combined below the annual Social Security wage base, 2.9% above it, plus an extra 0.9% employee-only Medicare tax above a fixed income threshold. Distributions from an S-corp are not subject to FICA. That tax difference is exactly why the IRS scrutinizes a low salary paired with a large distribution — it is the incentive to understate salary, not a loophole this calculator is built to help you exploit.

No warranty. This tool is free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice and does not replace a qualified CPA or tax attorney. It does not determine what your salary must be, file anything, or guarantee an outcome in an IRS examination — it is a starting-point estimate and a documentation aid, not a determination. FICA figures use the 2026 Social Security wage base ($184,500, per the Social Security Administration's own announcement) and current statutory rates, and assume this S-corp salary is your only wage income for the year. The comparable-wage figure is one you supply; this tool has no live wage-data source and does not verify it. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your specific facts with your own preparer. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This calculator vs. picking a round salary number

Most single-shareholder S-corp owners who haven't paid for a formal report set their own salary by picking a round number -- $50,000 because it sounds about right, whatever a friend in the same trade pays themselves, or last year's figure rolled forward unchanged. That number might be perfectly defensible. The problem is nothing has checked it against the comparable-wage test courts and the IRS actually apply, and that gap is the fact pattern in every reported reasonable-compensation adjustment case.

What each approach actually does

JobPicking a round numberThis calculator
How the number is setRounded to a figure that sounds reasonable, matches a peer, or repeats last year's number.Compared against a comparable-wage figure you supply, scaled to your actual hours.
Whether it's tied to the test that gets litigatedNot necessarily -- a round number is not itself evidence of the comparable-wage factor.Directly compares your planned salary to that factor and flags the gap.
Seeing the tax cost of the gapNot visible until a preparer or examiner runs the numbers separately.Shown immediately, in FICA-tax dollars, at your planned figure and at the comparable-wage floor.
A documentation trail if asked laterWhatever you remember about why you picked that figure.A nine-factor checklist you fill in and keep for your own records.
CostFree, no time spent beyond picking a number.Free, a few minutes to fill in the numbers you already have.
Where your numbers goNowhere -- it's a guess, not data.Nowhere -- stays in your browser's local storage, never uploaded.

Common questions

What's wrong with just picking a round number, like $50,000?

Nothing is wrong with the number itself -- $50,000 might even be defensible. What's missing is the comparison: a round number picked because it sounds reasonable, matches what a friend pays themselves, or is last year's figure rolled forward isn't tied to the comparable-wage test the IRS and courts actually apply (what would an unrelated employer pay someone else to do this specific job, for these specific hours). Watson v. Commissioner is exactly this pattern -- a round $24,000 salary against $200k-274k of annual profit, recharacterized because nobody had checked it against a market figure.

Isn't a round number faster than filling in a calculator?

Picking the number is faster, yes. What a round number skips is seeing the FICA-tax cost of the gap between what you picked and what a comparable role actually pays, and having a documented answer ready if your preparer or an examiner asks how the figure was set. This calculator takes the same couple of numbers you already have -- your planned salary, the business's compensation pool, and a comparable-wage figure you supply -- and runs the comparison and the tax math in the time it takes to fill in a form.

Does rolling last year's salary forward count as a documented method?

Not on its own. Rev. Rul. 74-44's factors include the comparable-wage test and the corporation's dividend history, not simply consistency with a prior year -- a salary that was never benchmarked to a market wage doesn't become benchmarked by being repeated. It can still be a reasonable number; the point is that nothing so far has checked it against the test that actually gets litigated.

Is my information safer with a round-number guess than with this calculator?

A guess never leaves your head, and this calculator never leaves your browser -- no account, no upload, and nothing sent to a server. The only difference is that one of the two gives you a comparison and a documentation checklist to keep.

This page names no specific product or service -- it compares against the generic method of picking a round salary figure without checking it against the comparable-wage test, not a competing tool.

This calculator vs. RCReports and a paid reasonable-compensation report

RCReports is the name most CPAs hear for a formal, purchasable reasonable-compensation report, and it does a genuinely different job from this page. This free calculator answers the question you have right now -- am I in a defensible range, and what would closing the gap cost in FICA tax -- with numbers you already have, no account and no fee. Here is exactly where each one fits.

What each one actually does

JobThis calculatorRCReports (paid, per report)
How the comparable-wage figure is sourcedYou supply it yourself -- from BLS OEWS, a trade salary survey, or your own judgment.Matched from a licensed occupational wage-survey database against your stated job duties, location, and hours.
OutputAn instant on-screen estimate, plus a nine-factor documentation checklist you fill in yourself.A formal, citable written report under a named methodology, typically produced by or for your CPA.
Where it's most usefulA first read on where you stand, or comparing the FICA cost of different salary levels before deciding.Documentation to keep in the client file, or evidence to produce if the IRS actually examines the return.
CostFree.Typically in the low hundreds of dollars per report.
Where your data goesNowhere -- stays in your browser's local storage, never uploaded.Collected and stored by the report service to produce and retain the document.

Common questions

What does a paid reasonable-compensation report like RCReports actually provide that this free calculator doesn't?

A formal report is built on licensed occupational wage-survey data (matched to your specific job duties, location, and hours), produced under a named methodology, and typically delivered as a citable document a CPA can put in a client's file or produce in an IRS examination as evidence the salary figure was researched rather than guessed. This calculator does none of that -- it takes a comparable-wage figure you supply yourself and runs the arithmetic and factor checklist around it instantly, for free.

When is a free self-check enough, and when do I need a formal paid report?

A free self-check is enough for an owner who wants a first read on where they stand, wants to see the FICA cost of different salary levels before deciding, or is nowhere close to a risky pattern (salary already close to or above a reasonable estimate, or no meaningful distribution being taken). A formal report earns its cost when the stakes are higher: a large distribution alongside a low salary, a pending or active IRS examination, or a CPA who wants a citable, licensed-data document in the client file rather than a number the client estimated themselves.

Does this calculator replace an accountant's judgment or a formal report?

No. It is a self-check and a documentation aid -- a place to see the arithmetic and record your own answers to the nine factors courts weigh. It does not access any wage-survey database, does not certify a figure, and is not something you would hand an examiner as evidence in place of your own preparer's work.

Is my financial data safer in this calculator than in a paid report service?

This calculator never uploads anything -- every number you enter stays in your browser's local storage and is never sent to a server. A paid report service necessarily collects your business and compensation details to produce and store the report; that's a reasonable tradeoff for the document you're paying for, but it's a tradeoff this calculator doesn't ask you to make.

why-the-irs-tests-your-s-corp-salary.htm.text:
← S-Corp Reasonable Compensation Calculator

Why does the IRS test your S-corp salary?

An S-corp doesn't pay corporate income tax on its profit — it passes through to the shareholder's own return. That makes the split between "W-2 salary" and "distribution" matter more than it would in a regular C-corp, because only the salary portion is subject to employment tax. Here is why the IRS watches that split, what the leading case actually decided, and why there is no shortcut percentage that makes the question go away.

Open the free reasonable-compensation calculator

The incentive the rule exists to police

Salary is subject to combined Social Security and Medicare tax (FICA) — 15.3% combined up to the year's Social Security wage base, 2.9% above it. A distribution from an S-corp's profit is not subject to FICA at all. So every dollar an owner recategorizes from "salary" to "distribution" saves roughly 15 cents in employment tax, with no change to income tax. That gap, not the S-corp structure itself, is what the reasonable-compensation rule is built to close.

Watson v. Commissioner, in brief

David Watson was a CPA and the sole shareholder-employee of his own accounting firm, organized as an S-corp. Over the two years at issue, the firm's profit ran approximately $200,000–274,000, and Watson paid himself exactly $24,000 in W-2 salary each year, taking the remainder as distributions. The Tax Court, upheld by the Eighth Circuit (668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012)), compared his pay to what an accountant of his experience would earn at a competing firm and to what his own firm would have had to pay to replace him, and found $24,000 unreasonable. It recharacterized $67,044 of each year's distributions as wages — creating a back payroll-tax assessment, plus penalties and interest, on money Watson had already spent as a distribution.

Why the "60/40 rule" is a myth

Advisor blogs and forum posts sometimes describe a "60/40 rule" — 60% of profit as salary, 40% as distribution — or similar percentage guidelines. The IRS has never published a safe-harbor percentage of any kind. Following a percentage rule does not itself establish that a salary is reasonable, and a salary that happens to match one is judged on the same comparable-wage facts as any other. Treat a percentage figure as a rough sanity check at most, never as documentation.

What the actual test looks at

Rev. Rul. 74-44 and the cases applying it (Watson; Sean McAlary Ltd. v. Commissioner; Glass Blocks Unlimited v. Commissioner) weigh a facts-and-circumstances test, not a formula: training and experience, the actual duties performed, time and effort devoted to the business, dividend history, what the business pays non-owner employees, the timing and manner of any bonus, what comparable businesses pay for similar services, and whether a documented formula or agreement sets compensation. The comparable-wage factor — what an unrelated employer would pay someone else for this job — is the one every reported case leans on most heavily, which is why this tool's calculator asks you to supply that figure directly rather than estimating it for you.

Distributions are not the problem — an artificially low salary paired with one is

Nothing about the reasonable-compensation rule discourages distributions after a defensible salary is paid; that split is a normal, expected feature of the S-corp structure and often the whole reason an owner chooses it. The exposure sits specifically in a salary set low enough, next to a distribution large enough, that the pattern reads as pay recharacterized to dodge FICA — the exact fact pattern in every reported adjustment case.

Common questions

Why does the IRS care how I split S-corp pay between salary and distributions?

Because the split changes how much employment tax is owed. Salary is subject to combined Social Security and Medicare tax (FICA), currently 15.3% combined up to the annual Social Security wage base and 2.9% above it. Distributions from an S-corp are not subject to FICA at all. An owner who calls most of their pay a "distribution" instead of salary can significantly understate their employment tax bill, which is exactly the incentive the reasonable-compensation rule exists to police.

What did Watson v. Commissioner actually decide?

David Watson, a CPA and the sole shareholder-employee of his accounting firm's S-corp, paid himself a $24,000 W-2 salary in each of two years while the firm's profit ran roughly $200,000–274,000, taking the rest as distributions. The Eighth Circuit upheld the Tax Court's finding that $24,000 was not reasonable compensation for a CPA of his experience doing that work, and recharacterized $67,044 of each year's distributions as wages — creating a back payroll-tax bill plus penalties and interest.

Is there an IRS safe-harbor percentage for S-corp salary, like 60% of profit?

No. The IRS has never published a safe-harbor percentage. The "60/40 rule" and similar percentage guidelines that circulate in online forums and some advisors' marketing are informal rules of thumb, not IRS guidance, and following one does not itself establish that a salary is reasonable.

What test does the IRS and the courts actually use?

A multi-factor, facts-and-circumstances comparable-wage test, drawn from Rev. Rul. 74-44 and applied in cases like Watson, Sean McAlary Ltd., and Glass Blocks Unlimited: what would an unrelated employer pay someone else to do this specific job, for these specific hours, weighed alongside training and experience, duties, dividend history, pay to other employees, and whether compensation follows a documented formula or agreement.

Does the reasonable-compensation rule mean I should never take distributions?

No. Distributions after a reasonable salary is paid are a normal, expected part of the S-corp structure and the reason many owners choose it. The rule targets a salary set artificially low specifically to shrink the FICA base while a much larger distribution is paid alongside it — not the existence of a distribution itself.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, or financial advice and does not replace a qualified CPA or tax attorney. Case summaries are provided for background only; verify any figure you rely on against the primary source and your own facts.
